name: Flame Scarlet
lede: Flame Scarlet is a vivid reddish orange that Robert Ridgway carried over from his own 1886 color nomenclature into the 1912 standard, and that the ISCC-NBS system later filed under "vivid reddish orange."

sections.title: A Ridgway orange
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* gives this hue at plate II, hue 9, carrying it over from his earlier 1886 nomenclature of colors [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 placed it in block 34, "vivid reddish orange" [2]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary is cited for the same block by the 1955 circular, though it does not add its own first-recorded date here [1].

The nearest named neighbor is [[mandarin|Mandarin]], 3.7 units away and duller; [[bright-orange|Bright Orange]] sits at the same distance but more vivid [2]. Ridgway's plate is a scan of an aged printed card, so the hex value is only an approximation of the original ink [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Flame Scarlet appears in 17 of our 23,781 paintings, as photographed, rarer than 61 percent of the named colors in the archive [3]. It peaks in the 1700s, in 6 of 3,449 paintings, at 1.6 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive, and is most over-represented in paintings from India, at 3.4 times expected [3]. Where it appears, it almost always plays an accent rather than a base color [3]. The earliest match, in a work attributed to Albrecht Dürer, is dated 1526 — 360 years before Ridgway's 1886 record of the name, which marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof that the same pigment was in use, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].
